title: How to Build a Budget with AI (Free, Step by Step)

scenes.sub: BLS Consumer Expenditures, per consumer unit (Oct 2026)

chips.text: 3 in 4: never used AI for money

scenes.text: In twenty twenty five, the average American household spent eighty one thousand, nine hundred and five dollars. That's about six thousand eight hundred dollars every single month, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Most of us couldn't say exactly where it all went. A free AI chatbot can sort a messy month of spending in minutes. Yet three in four Americans say they've never used AI for their money. In this video, I'll show you a step by step way to build a budget with AI, what to never paste into a chatbot, and where AI gets the math wrong.

scenes.chapterTitle: The rule: AI drafts, you decide
scenes.title: AI drafts. You decide.
scenes.sub: A budget in 3 steps, plus a safety rule
scenes.text: Here's the idea behind this whole video. AI is great at the boring parts of budgeting: sorting transactions into categories, adding them up, spotting repeat charges, and turning your goals into a draft plan. But it doesn't know your life, and it can make mistakes with numbers. So the rule is simple. AI drafts, you decide. We'll go through three steps. First, collect your spending safely. Second, let AI sort and summarize it. Third, turn that into a plan you'll actually follow. Then I'll show you a fifteen minute monthly check in that keeps it working.

scenes.chapterTitle: How many people use AI for money
scenes.text: First, where do people stand? In a Verasight survey of one thousand US adults in March twenty twenty six, about seventy five percent said they had never used AI to manage money or investments. Only about nine percent had made a saving, budgeting or spending decision based on AI. Still, interest is real. In a NerdWallet and Harris Poll survey from October twenty twenty five, forty eight percent of Americans said AI will have a positive impact on their personal finances, with younger adults far more positive than older ones. So people are curious, but cautious. And caution is the right instinct.

Step one is collecting your spending. Most banks and card apps let you download your transactions as a spreadsheet file, often called a CSV. Grab two or three months, so one odd month doesn't fool you. Before you share anything, delete the columns you don't need, like your name, account numbers and balances. Then paste just the date, the merchant and the amount into the chat, or upload the cleaned file if your chatbot allows files. Those three columns are enough. If you're worried about privacy, you can even round the amounts or rename the merchants. The AI only needs the pattern.

items.name: Account numbers
items.desc: Nobody needs them to sort spending

items.name: Passwords, PINs
items.desc: Never, to any chat or app

items.name: SSN
items.desc: It has nothing to do with a budget

items.name: Bank logins
items.desc: Never type them into a chat window

items.name: Privacy settings
items.desc: Turn off chat training if you can

footer.text: Share the pattern, not your identity

scenes.text: Here's the safety rule, and it matters more than any prompt. Never paste full account numbers or card numbers into a chatbot. Nobody needs them to sort your spending. Never share passwords or PINs, with any chat or app. Your Social Security number has nothing to do with a budget, so leave it out. Don't type your bank login into a chat window either. And check your chatbot's privacy settings. Some let you stop your chats from being used to train their models. Treat the chat like a conversation with a helpful stranger. Share the pattern of your spending, not your identity.

scenes.chapterTitle: Step 2: the prompt that sorts it

items.text: Mark each one: need or want

scenes.text: Step two is the prompt. You don't need anything fancy. Ask it to do four jobs. One, sort each line into simple categories like housing, groceries, eating out, transport and subscriptions. Two, total each category for each month. Three, flag every repeat charge, because forgotten subscriptions hide in plain sight. Four, mark each category as a need or a want, and let you correct it. Then ask one more question: what surprised you in this data? You'll often get a useful answer, like eating out costing more than you thought. Ask for the result as a table, so it's easy to check.

Once you have your totals, it helps to compare them with a benchmark. Here's how the average US household spent its money each month in twenty twenty five, based on the government's yearly figures. Housing, about two thousand three hundred dollars. Transportation, about eleven hundred. Food, about nine hundred. Insurance and pensions, which includes social security taxes, about eight hundred and fifty. Healthcare, about five hundred and forty. And entertainment, about three hundred and forty. These six add up to about six thousand dollars a month, and total spending was nearly eighty two thousand dollars for the year. Housing alone is about a third. Your numbers will differ, and that's fine. Look for the category that's way off for you.

scenes.chapterTitle: Step 3: turn the numbers into a plan

items.text: Set a savings goal, pay it first
Ask for 3 versions: easy, medium, strict

scenes.text: Step three is turning the numbers into a plan. Start with your fixed bills, like rent and insurance, because those barely move. Next, decide on a savings goal, and treat it like a bill you pay first. Then give every other category a monthly limit. Here's where AI really helps. Ask it for three versions of the plan, an easy one, a medium one, and a strict one, each showing exactly what changes. You might see that the easy version only trims eating out, while the strict one pauses three subscriptions. Then you pick. Remember the rule: AI drafts, you decide.

items.name: Generic tips

items.name: Old info
items.desc: Check rates and rules at the source

footer.text: Trust the draft, verify the totals

scenes.text: Now the honest part. AI is not a calculator you can blindly trust. Chatbots can make math slips when adding long lists, so re-add the totals in a spreadsheet or ask the AI to show its working. They can also fill gaps with made up numbers instead of asking you. They'll sometimes put a purchase in the wrong category, because one store can mean groceries or gifts. The advice can be generic, since it doesn't know your debts or goals unless you say so. And interest rates or tax rules it mentions may be out of date. So trust the draft, but verify the totals.

scenes.chapterTitle: Why the first sort pays off
scenes.badge: Example: $50 a month in forgotten charges

chips.text: Send it to your savings goal

scenes.text: Here's why that first sort is worth doing. Small repeat charges add up quietly. Say the AI flags fifty dollars a month in subscriptions and charges you forgot about. That's just an example, but cancel them and you free up six hundred dollars a year. The key is to cancel, not just pause or ignore them. Then point that money straight at your savings goal, ideally with an automatic transfer on payday, so it never sits in your checking account waiting to be spent. One sorting session can pay for itself many times over.

items.text: Compare each category with your limits

scenes.text: A budget only works if you look at it again. So here's a fifteen minute monthly check in. On the first weekend of each month, export last month's transactions and remove private details. Paste them in with the same prompt and the same categories, so the months are comparable. Ask the AI to compare each category with your limits and show what went over. Then adjust just one thing for next month, not ten. Small, steady changes stick far better than a dramatic plan you drop in week two. Consistency beats perfection.

scenes.title: AI drafts. You decide.
scenes.next: How to Plan Your Entire Week with AI in 15 Minutes
scenes.text: So that's the method. Collect safely, let AI sort and summarize, build a plan with three versions, then check in once a month. Now I want to hear from you. Which category surprised you most when you looked at your own spending? Tell me in the comments. If this helped, subscribe to Future Money Lab, and share it with someone who keeps saying they'll start a budget next month. In the next video, I'll show you how to plan your entire week with AI in fifteen minutes. Remember, this is education, not financial advice.

youtube.title: How to Build a Budget with AI (Free, Step by Step)
youtube.summary: The average US household spent $81,905 in 2025, about $6,800 a month, yet most people can't say where it went. This is a step-by-step guide to building a budget with a free AI chatbot: how to collect your spending safely, what to never paste into a chatbot, a simple prompt that sorts and totals your transactions, how your numbers compare with the average US household, how to turn them into a plan, where AI gets budgets wrong, and a 15-minute monthly check-in.
youtube.details:
Numbers mentioned (checked November 2026):
- Average annual expenditures per US consumer unit, 2025: $81,905 (about $6,825 a month); housing $27,790 (33.9%), transportation $13,492, food $10,633, personal insurance and pensions $10,175, healthcare $6,470, entertainment $4,084 (BLS Consumer Expenditures 2025, released October 29, 2026). Monthly figures in the video are these yearly figures divided by 12.
- 74.7% of US adults have not used AI to manage money or investments; 8.9% made a saving, budgeting or spending decision based on AI (Verasight, n=1,000, March 2026).
- 48% of Americans say AI will have a positive impact on their personal finances (NerdWallet / The Harris Poll, n=2,084, October 2025).
- $50 a month = $600 a year is an illustration only.
